item.title: The Takaichi government is increasingly resembling an extremist cult: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 23:53:00
Militaristic emblem Illustration: Liu Rui/GT It is precisely because the Takaichi government has tolerated and encouraged these forces that right-wing elements in Japanese politics are becoming more brazen than ever. They have even constructed a narrative of a "holy war for history," attempting to repackage the specter of militarism as a "spiritual legacy" of which the Japanese people should be proud. An increasingly dangerous Japan has long been on the radar of its neighbors, who remain wary of its actions. On Saturday, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made an offering to the Yasukuni Shrine as prime minister. This marked the fourth time this year that Takaichi had made an offering or donated ritual funds to the war criminals' shrine, a frequency rarely seen among Japan's former prime ministers. On the same day, several cabinet ministers and lawmakers also visited the shrine to pay their respects. The pattern of "the prime minister sending offerings while her subordinates make the pilgrimage" is becoming a familiar ritual in Takaichi's cabinet. Some Japanese right-wing figures argue that Takaichi has not visited the shrine in her capacity as prime minister since taking office, as if this were sufficient to address concerns over Japan's historical record. Yet Takaichi refrains from visiting in person while making offerings in the name of the prime minister; cabinet ministers and senior Liberal Democratic Party officials make the pilgrimage on her behalf, while she pays her respects from afar. Tokyo is pursuing an opportunistic strategy: Preserving its right-wing support base, avoiding the political fallout of a direct visit, and exploiting historical revisionism to justify military expansion and preparations for war. In fact, during nearly a year in office, Takaichi has consistently sent signals to Japan's domestic right-wing forces, seeking to systematically erode the postwar consensus against war, undermine the legitimacy of Japan's pacifist constitution, and lay the psychological groundwork for constitutional revision, military buildup, and arms expansion. The Takaichi government seems particularly fond of such deceptive tactics. Japan has repeatedly sent the wrong signals on the Taiwan question, effectively closing the door to dialogue while proclaiming internationally that it is "willing to communicate with China." More recently, Takaichi has described China as an "important neighbor" while refusing to retract her erroneous remarks on the Taiwan question. On the one hand, she is publicly putting on a show of eagerness to travel to Shenzhen to attend the APEC meeting. On the other, she is staging a political charade of her own, hinting that the Diet might not approve her attendance. These deceptive maneuvers are, in essence, attempts to exploit ambiguities and find room to maneuver for Tokyo's risky drive toward remilitarization. It is precisely because the Takaichi government has tolerated and encouraged these forces that right-wing elements in Japanese politics are becoming more brazen than ever. They have even constructed a narrative of a "holy war for history," attempting to recast Japan's war of aggression during World War II as a supposedly righteous campaign to "liberate Asia" and portray Class-A war criminals, whose hands were stained with the blood of people across Asia, as "spirits of the war dead who sacrificed themselves for their country." Cabinet members and lawmakers under Takaichi's government frequently visit sites associated with war criminals, using their political power to lend legitimacy to this "holy war" narrative and whip up public support for military expansion and preparations for war. Through repeated offerings, shrine visits, and a sustained propaganda campaign, they seek to gradually erase the just verdicts of the Tokyo Trial and repackage the specter of militarism as a "spiritual legacy" of which the Japanese people should be proud. More alarming still, this "holy war for history" narrative is closely intertwined with the Takaichi government's efforts to revise Japan's pacifist constitution and dramatically expand its military capabilities and preparations for war. This exposes the Takaichi government's deeply extremist, cult-like nature. Once historical responsibility for wartime atrocities is recast as "national sacrifice," the pacifist constitution can be portrayed as "a shackle holding back the nation's development," and military expansion and preparations for war can be given a supposedly "legitimate" justification. The erosion of historical understanding ultimately leads to a shift in national security strategy. This is precisely the most insidious and dangerous path toward Japan's remilitarization. Japanese politicians have openly discussed introducing nuclear-powered submarines and allowing US forces to bring nuclear weapons into Japan, while the "Three Non-Nuclear Principles" - a cornerstone of Japan's postwar nuclear policy commitments to the international community - have come under increasing pressure. Some Japanese right-wing figures believe they can blur the line between history and present-day realities, invoke "threats from neighboring countries" as a pretext for military expansion, and dress up that expansion as a reasonable national security measure. They seem to think this will allow them to pull the wool over the world's eyes and dismantle the postwar order in its entirety under the international community's very nose. But since Takaichi took office, Japan's relations with neighboring countries have deteriorated sharply. China, South Korea, and other countries that suffered under Japanese aggression have repeatedly lodged strong protests over her shrine-related actions and historically revisionist remarks, while expressing clear concerns about her moves to push beyond Japan's established exclusively defense-oriented policy. Russia and North Korea, too, remain highly vigilant about Japan's military buildup, preparations for war, and efforts to repudiate the postwar order, having issued explicit warnings through diplomatic channels on multiple occasions. An increasingly dangerous Japan has long been on the radar of its neighbors, who remain wary of its actions. Tokyo will find it far from easy to get away with its "deception tactics." Masahiko Shimizu, a professor of constitutional law at Nippon Sport Science University, has bluntly stated that Japanese politicians visiting Yasukuni Shrine is akin to German leaders tending Adolf Hitler's grave - a blatant desecration of historical justice. The analogy may not be entirely precise, but it is one that the US and Western public opinion, which have long tolerated the rhetoric and actions of Japan's right wing and even lent credibility to Japan's "peaceful" facade, would do well to heed. The 14 Class-A war criminals from WWII were convicted of war crimes by an international tribunal in accordance with the law. The wars of aggression they planned, launched, and carried out inflicted immense suffering on countries across Asia. As long as Japanese politicians continue to pay homage to these war criminals, this chapter of history can absolutely not truly be closed. No matter how the Takaichi government tries to repackage its actions or twist the facts, any attempt to whitewash militarism or resume military expansion will ultimately expose its dangerous nature before the entire world, provoking resolute opposition and ending in complete failure.

item.title: China's Long March rockets carry forward historic grit for new space exploration
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 23:53:00
At 12:15 pm July 10, 2026, Beijing time, the Long March 10B carrier rocket lifts off from the Hainan commercial space launch site, successfully placing its satellite payload into the designated orbit and completing its maiden flight mission. Photo: Fan Wei/GT Footage released Sunday by the China Manned Space Agency captures astronauts conducting research and daily work aboard China's Tiangong space station, including a rice-growing trial aiming for a harvest in orbit. Behind these orbital achievements lies the enduring Long March spirit. Borrowing its name from the Red Army's epic expedition, China's Long March rocket series embodies that pioneering grit, carrying space hardware into orbit while pushing forward reusable rocket innovation. These scenes reflect how far China's space capabilities have developed, from crewed flight to a space station in orbit and efforts to master reusable rockets. The name has become one of the most recognizable in Chinese aerospace sector, supporting crewed missions, launching BeiDou navigation satellite constellations, lunar and Mars exploration, and space station construction, Wang Yanan, editor-in-chief of Beijing-based Aerospace Knowledge magazine, told the Global Times on Sunday. Decades of development and successive breakthroughs have made the rocket program itself a technological Long March spanning generations, he said. A Long March into space The year 2026 marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, the epic military trek from 1934 to 1936 that broke through the encirclement of Kuomintang forces. Some participants marched as far as 12,500 kilometers, helping lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution, according to the Xinhua News Agency. The rockets bearing its name reached another milestone on October 10, when a Long March-12 placed the 27th batch of low-Earth orbit internet satellites into their planned orbit. It was the Long March family's 671st launch, Xinhua reported. The first came on April 24, 1970, when a Long March-1 rocket carried Dongfanghong-1, China's first artificial satellite, into space. That first flight followed years of work under difficult conditions. China began developing the launcher in the 1960s to send Dongfanghong-1 into orbit, when its industrial base was weak and access to key technologies was tightly restricted from abroad, according to Xinhua. "Naming the launch vehicle 'Long March' meant that, like the Red Army on the Long March, it would overcome every difficulty and ultimately achieve victory," Han Houjian, who worked on the Long March-1's overall design, recalled, according to Xinhua. At a media briefing on September 21, Long Lehao, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering and a launch vehicle expert at China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation, traced the name to a proposal by pioneering Chinese scientist Qian Xuesen on May 31, 1966. The name "Long March" conveyed the idea that developing China's launch vehicles was a new Long March toward the stars, Long said, quoting Qian. "Just as the Red Army had endured countless hardships on its 12,500-kilometer trek, China's rocket developers would have to overcome formidable obstacles, with the same conviction that their efforts would ultimately lead to success," he added. Since the first launch, the family has progressed from carrying one satellite at a time to deploying 41 in a single mission. It has also expanded the range of spacecraft it can launch and advanced from expendable vehicles toward reusable designs, Long said. These advances give the name a meaning beyond historical remembrance, Kang Guohua, a senior member of the Chinese Society of Astronautics and a professor of aerospace engineering at Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, told the Global Times on Sunday. Just as the Red Army fought to break through encirclement, China's space program has repeatedly had to find a way through external restrictions, he said. Kang cited the development of BeiDou and China's own space station as examples of breakthroughs achieved amid outside competition and technological barriers. China's space sector faced hostility and restrictions from the US and other Western countries from its earliest days, he said, while Long March rockets provided the means to carry that technological struggle forward. Naming the family after the Long March could hardly be more fitting, he added. From smaller launchers to the powerful Long March-5, and from conventional propellants to cleaner alternatives, the family has continued to evolve. Its vehicles now meet launch needs in low and high Earth orbits and deep space, carrying satellites, crewed spacecraft and probes on missions that underpin China's pursuit of self-reliance in space technology, Xinhua reported. The journey ahead That pursuit continues as China prepares for a more demanding phase of space development. The Long March rockets of today already differ greatly from those of decades ago, Wang said. Future versions will need to be larger and more capable, supporting more frequent launches, heavier payloads and a more sustainable launch program. Wang drew a parallel with the historical Long March: reaching northern Shaanxi did not mark the end of the Chinese revolution, and the rocket family's achievements are likewise milestones along a continuing journey. Earlier breakthroughs opened a new chapter, he said, but the space program now faces fresh challenges as its goals grow more ambitious and the demands on its launch vehicles increase. Two missions this year show how the next stage is taking shape. On June 1, a Long March-12B made its maiden flight from a commercial launch pad in the Dongfeng Commercial Aerospace Innovation Pilot Zone, delivering the 10th constellation of Qianfan satellites into orbit. Designed to serve commercial demand, including the deployment of large internet constellations, the reusable rocket has a single core stage about four meters in diameter and can carry out missions to different orbits. Its development emphasizes performance, safety, efficiency and lower costs, according to Science and Technology Daily, a Chinese media that focused on technology. A further milestone followed on July 10, when a Long March 10B carrier rocket lifted off from the Hainan commercial space launch site, successfully placing its satellite payload into the designated orbit and completing its maiden flight mission. Approximately six minutes after the separation of the rocket's first and second stages, the first stage made a controlled vertical descent and was successfully recovered through a net-based capture system on an offshore recovery platform located more than 300 kilometers away from the launch site. The first-stage recovery mission was completed successfully. The mission marked China's first successful controlled recovery of a launch vehicle's first stage and also the world's first net-based recovery of a launch vehicle. The Long March 10B carrier rocket has become China's first reusable launch vehicle to successfully complete a recovery mission. Like the historic Long March, China's rocket program has broken through external barriers and achieved important victories, Wang said, adding that as of now, greater ambitions now bring fresh challenges: China's expanding plans in space require more frequent launches, greater payload capacity and a more sustainable launch program, placing new demands on the Long March family - developing reusable, heavier and more advanced models. The Long March into space is not only a journey for China. "Reaching orbit is only stage one in humanity's exploration of space, our journey will continue to other planets and deeper into the universe," Wang said, "and that journey will also be a Long March for all humanity."

item.title: EU reportedly proposes new curbs on Chinese imports; trade deficit blame misplaced: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 23:47:00
The European Union (EU) flags in front of EU headquarters in Brussels, Belgium. Photo: VCG European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Friday that the EU would propose new restrictions on Chinese imports beyond the scope of a previously agreed arrangement on hybrid cars, citing the bloc's growing trade deficit with China as pretext, according to Reuters. Chinese experts, however, said the EU was blaming China for trade imbalances while overlooking its own export restrictions, high energy costs and industrial competitiveness problems. They warned that treating trade talks as a bargaining chip and import curbs as leverage would only drive up costs for European businesses and consumers, adding that Brussels should not underestimate China's resolve and ability to safeguard its own interests. Speaking after a European Council summit, Von der Leyen claimed that the EU's goods trade deficit with China was running at more than 1 billion euros ($1.12 billion) a day. She argued that the existing agreement would not resolve what she described as a structural imbalance. The European Commission i s also due to make a proposal in December to limit EU companies' reliance on single sources for certain critical supplies. Zhou Mi, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, told the Global Times that Von der Leyen's claim on the 1 billion euros in daily trade deficit risks stirring public sentiment rather than explaining the real impact on businesses and consumers. "If unilateral restrictions are imposed, they would undermine respect for WTO rules and erode trust in China-EU trade talks," he said. EU ignores its own problems "Simply focusing on the trade deficit, especially by repeatedly hyping its scale, does not necessarily explain its actual impact and may distort public perceptions," Zhou said. Trade involves businesses and consumers with different needs, Zhou said. Importers and exporters make decisions based on their own commercial interests, while the overall trade balance does not show how the benefits of those transactions are distributed among individual market participants. Also, China-EU trade is not limited to goods. According to China's statistics cited by China's ambassador to the EU, Cai Run, China ran a service trade deficit of $48.3 billion with the EU in 2025, and the bloc accounted for 41.6 percent of that deficit. China also paid the EU more than $10 billion in intellectual property fees. Jian Junbo, a professor at Fudan University's Center for China-Europe Relations, told the Global Times that the trade imbalance ultimately reflected differences in industrial capacity and competitiveness. China's stronger manufacturing capacity gives its products an edge in the market, while high energy costs, innovation gaps and technological constraints have weighed on the competitiveness of European industries. He also pointed to a contradiction in the EU's approach: Brussels wants to expand exports to China while restricting exports of certain products, including lithography machines. EU's high energy costs and weak industrial competitiveness are at the root of Europe's trade woes. The European Commission's 2026 Annual Single Market and Competitiveness Report identifies high energy costs and barriers within the single market among the issues facing European businesses. These domestic pressures are also relevant to the bloc's ability to compete internationally. High energy costs and weaknesses in industrial competitiveness are issues Brussels needs to address at home. Restricting imports may shield some producers from competition in the short term, but it will not lower energy costs, raise productivity or make European products more competitive in China, Jian said. The Chinese Ministry of Commerce has urged the EU to approach trade consultations with sincerity and resolve differences through dialogue. Responding to the EU's proposed dual-track approach toward China, a ministry spokesperson said the purpose of China-EU trade consultations was to properly manage differences and accommodate each other's concerns. "Both sides should demonstrate sincerity in resolving problems. The EU should not expect to gain benefits through pressure, and should not underestimate China's resolve and capability to safeguard its own interests," the spokesperson said. EU's pressure tactics will backfire Zhou said China-EU trade is based on complementary economic strengths, with businesses on both sides benefiting from access to each other's markets. Chinese imports help European companies obtain competitively priced goods and components, manage supply-chain uncertainty and ease inflationary pressures. Restricting those imports could increase costs for European manufacturers and consumers, he said, while doing little to resolve the bloc's underlying economic problems. Zhou said the economic consequences of trade should be assessed through the interests of businesses and consumers on both sides, rather than the overall deficit alone. Importers and exporters engage in trade to meet their own commercial needs, he said. Treating the deficit itself as proof that China-EU trade is unfair risks overlooking the benefits that businesses on both sides derive from those transactions. The EU cannot expect China to make concessions while it continues to prepare new restrictions and leaves China's concerns unresolved. Using market access as a bargaining chip risks turning trade consultations into a contest of pressure, making a lasting agreement harder to reach. If Brussels wants to improve trade relations, it needs to address the concerns of both sides rather than expect China alone to accommodate Europe's demands, experts said. Jian warned that expanding import restrictions could have far-reaching consequences for European businesses and consumers. Many Chinese imports are intermediate goods used in production, and replacing them with supplies from other sources could significantly raise costs and weaken European companies' competitiveness. Consumers would also face higher living costs as access to affordable goods diminishes, potentially adding to inflationary pressure. Some western media outlets have also questioned whether trade barriers can solve Europe's industrial problems. In an October commentary, the Financial Times noted that Chinese imports put competitive pressure on some European industries while providing competitively priced inputs to others. It called for reforms to strengthen Europe's long-term competitiveness. Zhou warned that unilateral measures would undermine the foundations of trade and mutual trust, as well as respect for WTO rules. Differences between China and the EU should be addressed through established consultation mechanisms, he said. A confrontational approach, Zhou added, would make it harder for Europe to achieve its own economic goals.

item.title: When 'strategic partner' means different things in Washington and New Delhi
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 22:19:00
US, India Illustration:Chen Xia/GT The US-India relationship has once again laid bare the exercise of great power leverage - Washington is playing an ancient game: first using strategic commitments to take you hostage, then using economic coercion to suppress you. Indian media reports say US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is about to visit India, marking his second visit this year. Washington wants to talk about a "strategic partnership," while New Delhi wants to talk about tariffs. The two sides are working from completely different menus. Nine months have passed, and the US-India trade framework agreement reached in February remains unsigned. India's finance minister says negotiations have hit a "plateau." The US Trade Representative says an announcement is "not imminent." Translation: they're stuck, and neither side is willing to budge further. Washington's rhetoric has always been polished. Through references to the "Indo-Pacific Strategy", shared values and the Quad - Washington portrays India as its most trusted partner in the Asia-Pacific. But when it comes to trade realities, the tone shifts: high tariffs on Indian steel, sustained pressure on Indian pharmaceuticals, barriers against Indian IT services. Meanwhile, Japan, South Korea, and Australia are receiving far more favorable treatment during the same period. This tells us a lot about the problem. Washington ranks its "strategic partners" by usefulness. When it needs India to take sides in the Indo-Pacific, it calls you a partner; when it needs to protect its own industries, the tariff club swings freely. Japan and South Korea are military allies; Australia is part of the "Five Eyes"; India, in Washington's ledger, is simply a card whose value can be adjusted at any time. What particularly alarms New Delhi is that the current US administration is demanding that India take three major steps: reduce Russian oil purchases, open agricultural markets, and increase American energy imports. And reportedly, this time they want India to buy more Venezuelan oil - oil over which the US has already established monopoly control. Each demand is no minor matter. Energy security affects the nation's lifeline; agriculture involves the livelihoods of hundreds of millions of small farmers; Russian oil helps keep costs down for Indian industry. US' subtext is clear: You must play by my rules. It's hard to believe such demands come from a "partner." Of course, the US has long used geopolitical leverage to "manipulate" its relationship with India, using the Quad and the "Indo-Pacific Strategy" to reinforce India's position while trying to restrict India's room for maneuver. But India has not fully accepted the hand dealt. For India, the value of being designated an American "strategic partner" is diminishing. Meanwhile, with tariff policies mired in legal challenges, India is even more hesitant to make commitments - will policy change again next year? India's exports have grown strongly in 2026. If American tariffs rise back to 25 percent, that growth trajectory will be destroyed. India would rather not sign an agreement than accept terms that damage its long-term prospects. So the situation has become this: the US applies pressure; India drags its feet. The delay is not passive submission - it is a form of resistance with boundaries. India cannot easily abandon US' security card, but it refuses to put all its chips on the table. The trade agreement remains unsigned for this reason. Whether this agreement gets signed or not, India has already seen through America's real agenda. Behind this lies a larger question: What does Washington's "strategic partnership" actually offer India? India's example makes the answer clear. The US doesn't want an equal partner - it wants a partner willing to follow its strategic lead and sacrifice economic interests on American terms. The moment the other side's interests conflict with American domestic politics, "partnership" gives way to tariffs. Such a relationship is difficult for any nation conscious of its own interests to accept long-term. For India, the American "strategic partner" label is losing value. This doesn't mean India will turn toward some other great power. Still, it means New Delhi will more firmly chart its own course, strengthen ties with Russia, Iran, and others, and place "strategic autonomy" more prominently in its dealings with major powers. The deadlock in US-India trade negotiations is more than a commercial dispute. It exposes the limits of a model of relations between major powers: prioritizing exploitation over equality; demanding cooperation while denying respect. How far such a relationship can go - India is answering that question in its own way.

item.title: France rocked by nationwide unrest as protests turn violent with more than 2,000 arrested
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 21:56:00
Demonstrators face off with law enforcement officers during a protest in Paris, France, on October 17, 2026. Photo: Xinhua Burning cars, shattered shop windows and clouds of tear gas filled the streets of Paris on Saturday as nationwide protests over soaring living costs and deteriorating public services descended into violent clashes across France. More than 2,000 people have been arrested during violent protests across France on Saturday, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said Sunday. More than 600 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters have been injured in the violence so far, he said, citing provisional figures. The unrest, described by Reuters as some of the worst violence France has witnessed in decades, spread to major cities including Marseille, Lyon and Lille, where masked groups set buildings ablaze, ransacked shops and stormed government offices, Reuters reported. In Paris, groups of masked protesters torched parked vehicles, smashed storefronts and looted shops as riot police deployed water cannons and tear gas to disperse crowds. Entire streets in the capital had been "devastated," Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said, according to AFP. In the central French city of Limoges, masked rioters set fire to the historic City Hall, built in 1883, after torching a police vehicle and smashing windows to enter the building. Flames engulfed the 143-year-old landmark, causing its roof to collapse and destroying around two-thirds of its facade. Local prefect Maurice Barate described the destruction as a "catastrophe of heritage," saying the building was largely lost, according to France 24. In the southern port city of Marseille, protesters forced their way into City Hall, overturning a bust of Marianne, a symbol of the French Republic, and smashing furniture before being driven out by police. Several protesters sought to draw parallels with the French Revolution of 1789, according to the AFP. "It's the Revolution - we're taking the Bastille!" some shouted in Marseille during the forced entry into the mayor's offices. In the western city of La Rochelle, marchers streamed behind a placard reading: "Revolution or death." And in the southern city of Montpellier, a giant blue sign reading "The people will win" was unfurled above a central square. French President Emmanuel Macron vowed on X that "those who carried out vandalism, attacked administrative offices or businesses, or carried out looting - even in our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished." Opposition politicians vying to replace Macron in presidential elections in April and May next year seized on the chaos. Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen condemned "the rioters" and claimed that the party of her far-left rival for the presidency, Jean-Luc Melenchon, had "legitimized the violence." She said on X that, if she came to power, she would protect the French "from the violence of the extreme left." Melenchon, who had prominently supported the demonstrations and the student protests preceding them, urged demonstrators to stay away from any looting, describing it as "contrary to our methods." France's Yellow Vest movement, which eight years ago staged street protests against Macron's government over planned fuel tax hikes, had called for Saturday's "yellow and youth" demonstrations. The latest unrest follows weeks of student-led protests that began on September 17 in Créteil, a southeastern suburb of Paris, before spreading across France. The movement was initially driven by complaints over teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms, deteriorating school facilities and overloaded timetables, according to a statement by French high school students' union Union Syndicale Lycéenne (USL), cited by Le Monde on September 29. The protests subsequently escalated into confrontations with police in several cities, including Strasbourg, Lyon and Rennes, where officers fired tear gas while some protesters set fires in the streets and hurled projectiles, Reuters reported on October 6. According to a survey released on October 8 by French research institute L'ObSoCo in partnership with Sciences Po's political research center CEVIPOF, 45 percent of French respondents cited inflation and purchasing power among their main concerns, reflecting mounting pressure from rising energy and living costs. The French government has pledged measures to address students' grievances, including the deployment of around 3,000 additional teachers to ease staffing shortages, Al Jazeera reported on October 8. The unrest comes ahead of France's presidential election, scheduled for April 18 and May 2, 2027, according to the French government's official election schedule and the constitution published by the Élysée Palace. Beyond the immediate violence, the unrest has exposed deeper strains in French society, from mounting economic pressures and deteriorating public services to growing political polarization. Chinese experts told the Global Times that years of unresolved structural problems, compounded by fiscal constraints, have left the government with limited room to address public grievances, while the approaching 2027 presidential election could further sharpen political divisions. Chen Hong, director of the Institute of Region and Country Studies at East China Normal University, told the Global Times that the unrest reflects structural pressures in France's economic and social model. Sluggish growth and fiscal constraints have strained public services, while unequal opportunities have fueled frustration and distrust of political elites. Looking ahead to the 2027 presidential election, Chen said the unrest could deepen political divisions, with the left emphasizing social welfare and wealth redistribution and the right focusing on security and order. The greater challenge, he argued, is whether France's next leadership can offer credible reforms and rebuild public trust. Dong Yifan, an associate research fellow at the Academy of Country and Area Studies at Beijing Language and Culture University, said that compared with the Yellow Vest movement in 2018, France now faces greater economic and social pressures. He noted that limited reforms have failed to address underlying problems, while mounting fiscal constraints have restricted the government's ability to increase spending on public services and other livelihood-related priorities. Dong said France has a long tradition of street protests as a means of expressing public grievances. With the government preparing its budget for the coming year and Macron approaching the end of his presidency, the latest demonstrations also reflect growing public pressure for political and social change ahead of the 2027 presidential election. With high public debt and persistent budget deficits forcing the government to tighten spending, its ability to address longstanding inequalities in education and public services has become increasingly constrained, Qian Feng, an international affairs expert with the Tsinghua University said. Qian also warned that the turmoil could intensify political polarization ahead of the 2027 presidential election, as rival political forces seek to capitalize on public discontent. Disputes over fiscal austerity, immigration, public security and deteriorating public services could become central election issues, potentially deepening divisions within French society.

item.title: GT Voice: India should move beyond deficit anxiety as trade with China rises
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 21:03:00
China, India Illustration: Xia Qing/GT The latest China-India trade figures again thrusts the economic relationship into the media spotlight. India's bilateral trade with China rose nearly 29 percent year-on-year to reach $91.76 billion in the April-September period, making China the largest trading partner of India in the first half of the 2026-27 financial year, according to India's Commerce Ministry. The rising momentum of China-India trade is a positive development both sides should treasure. Yet behind the impressive numbers, India's anxiety about its trade deficit with China remains clearly visible. Frankly speaking, India's long-running trade deficit with China is a structural phenomenon shaped over the years by the two countries' industrial structures and comparative advantages. India is by no means short of competitive industries. From its fast-rising electronics assembly capacity to globally recognized pharmaceutical intermediate products, specialty agricultural products and textile goods, India holds a lot of cards that it can use to compete internationally. But having competitive industries is not the same as delivering a surge in exports to China. For a very long time, the basic pattern of China-India trade saw China ship large volumes of electromechanical equipment, electronic components and industrial intermediates to India, while India exported iron ore, seafood and other resource-based and primary goods to China. This division of labor was the natural outcome of the two countries' different stages of industrialization. If India wants to gradually ease its trade deficit, the key lies in tapping its own potential and turning its competitive industries into products that the Chinese market demands. What makes this moment different is that China's ongoing push for high-end, intelligent manufacturing upgrading and continued opening-up of its services sectors have opened unprecedented new window of opportunities for India. The massive new demand generated across these fields can easily become the core direction for India to cultivate new export growth points to China. Rather than competing for shares in traditional primary product categories, aligning export portfolios with the trajectory of China's industrial upgrade represents a more pragmatic and sustainable path forward. Signs of progress in this direction are emerging. According to Chinese customs data, China's imports from India surged 40.7 percent year-on-year in the January-September period, far outpacing average trade growth. This clearly shows that India's exports to China are gradually finding a direction suited to the Chinese market. The real question before India is whether it can sustain this round of growth, extend breakthroughs in a few sectors to more industrial tracks, and turn short-term export gains into long-term domestic manufacturing competitiveness. Some in India simply attribute the trade deficit with China to market access issues, and even go so far as to claim that "non-tariff barriers remain the biggest obstacle" to bilateral trade. But if access to the Chinese market was riddled with barriers to the extent that some claim, how could India's exports to China have grown by more than 40 percent? Viewed from another perspective, such voices actually reflect a growing awareness across Indian circles of how important the Chinese market is to the future of Indian manufacturing, along with a strong eagerness among Indian exporters to expand their footprint in China. China's overall level of opening-up has been substantial, and India's high export growth was delivered under the current open trade framework ̵ a fact that speaks far louder than any debate. Blaming trade deficit entirely on alleged external barriers risks covering up real shortcomings in product competitiveness, channel development, and international standard alignment. This approach does nothing to solve the actual problem, and will only work against the healthy development of bilateral trade relations. In the long run, there remains ample room to deepen China-India economic cooperation, and the two sides can certainly move forward together on the basis of mutual benefit and reciprocity to make the pie bigger. The economic relationship between two countries should not be defined by a single deficit figure. Volumes are rising, exports are growing, and the willingness of both sides to expand cooperation is strengthening, which are all encouraging signs. What needs to be done is to let the potential continue to materialize and make mutual benefit and reciprocity the shared guiding principles.

item.title: World's longest cross-sea high-speed rail bridge sees closure of first navigation channel span

Published: 2026-10-18 20:45:00
The southern navigation channel bridge of the Hangzhou Bay Cross-Sea Railway Bridge achieves closure on October 17, 2026. Photo: Screenshot from People's Daily As the steel truss girder of the southern navigation channel bridge of the Hangzhou Bay Cross-Sea Railway Bridge saw closure on Saturday evening, it became the first of the three navigation channel bridges to reach this milestone, marking a landmark breakthrough in the construction of the world's longest cross-sea high-speed railway bridge. This achievement has laid a solid foundation for subsequent stay-cable tensioning, bridge deck construction, and the full structural system conversion of the entire bridge. The bridge forms a crucial section of the Nantong-Ningbo High Speed Railway. At 29.2 kilometers, it is currently the world's longest and highest-standard clustered cross-sea railway bridge under construction, according to the People's Daily. The project consists of northern, central, and southern navigation channel bridges, as well as mid-sea approach bridges and shoal-area approach bridges. The southern navigation channel bridge that has just been closed is situated in the central waters of Hangzhou Bay. It measures 814.5 meters in total length, with a main span of 364 meters capable of accommodating vessels of up to 3,000 deadweight tons, said the report. Hangzhou Bay is one of the world's three strongest tidal bays, with a maximum tidal range of nearly nine meters, swift currents, and frequent strong winds. The annual effective offshore construction window is extremely limited. The highly saline and humid environment, together with constantly shifting seabed scouring and deposition, poses extreme challenges to construction precision, structural safety and offshore operations. To overcome the world-class construction difficulties, the project team has adopted an innovative double-sided incremental launching closure technique suited to the complex conditions of a bay with strong tides. During construction, BeiDou Navigation Satellite System positioning and digital monitoring systems were employed, with comprehensive monitoring points installed on the towers, steel girders, and temporary supports. Stress, cable force, and displacement data were collected at millisecond intervals. Besides, longitudinal wind-resistant devices and transverse restrainers were used to dynamically adjust the alignment of the closure gap. Operations were deliberately scheduled during nighttime periods of stable temperature to minimize thermal deformation. In addition, the project team has established a meteorological and hydrological early-warning mechanism and dynamically optimized the construction schedule to ensure offshore safety. Following the closure of the southern navigation channel bridge, the project will proceed with graded release of stay cables, casting of wet joints, installation and tensioning of the remaining cables, and placement of permanent bearings, steadily advancing the full structural system conversion. All offshore pile foundations and pier shafts of the bridge have been completed. Construction of the main structures of the three navigation channel bridges is progressing steadily, and overall works across the line are accelerating. The Nantong- Ningbo High Speed Railway, with a total length of 301 kilometers, forms an important part of the coastal corridor in China's high-speed rail network. Once completed, it will significantly densify the rapid rail network in the Yangtze River Delta, shorten the travel times between coastal cities in Jiangsu and Zhejiang provinces, improve the regional comprehensive transportation system and further inject strong momentum into the region's high-quality integrated development. Global Times

item.title: Researchers identify world's 1st known juvenile fossil of Huphsuchus dating back around 247 mln years in C. China's Hubei
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 16:22:00
Reconstruction of a juvenile Huphsuchus in its natural habitat Photo: Courtesy of Hubei Institute of Geosciences An international collaborative study has recently confirmed the world’s first juvenile fossil of Huphsuchus, an extinct genus of small marine reptiles dating back approximately 247 million years, discovered in Yuan’an county, Central China’s Hubei Province, the Global Times learned from the Hubei Institute of Geosciences, Hubei Geological Bureau, on Sunday. The research has been published in the Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society. Wang Yinuo of Peking University, and Zou Yarui, a senior engineer from the Hubei Institute of Geosciences, Hubei Geological Bureau, are the paper’s co-first authors. Researched and named in 1972 by Chinese paleontologist Yang Zhongjian, Huphsuchus was a prehistoric marine reptile that lived in shallow marine waters during the Early Triassic, approximately 247 million years ago. The genus represents one of the early evolutionary branches of reptiles that diversified into marine environments following the end-Permian mass extinction. More than 50 years of research has found Huphsuchus fossils only near the border of Yuan’an and Nanzhang counties in Hubei. However, as nearly all known specimens are adults, some researchers have suggested that its juveniles may be the same species as Nanchangosaurus, fossils of which were discovered in the same geological strata in the area and first reported in 1959. In 2023, the Hubei Institute of Geosciences began ecological restoration and emergency fossil excavations at Yinggou Quarry, a major marine reptile fossil site in Yuan’an county. During quarry slope clearance, researchers discovered a partially preserved fossil skeleton, designated YGM17-1, in the fossil-bearing layer numbered 17. After careful restoration and examination, researchers confirmed that the specimen belonged to a juvenile Huphsuchus, rather than Nanchangosaurus or other marine reptiles. According to Zou, the research team conducted detailed morphological and comparative anatomical studies of the specimen, confirming that it was distinct from Nanchangosaurus and exhibited the characteristic features of Huphsuchus, including 10 cervical vertebrae and 26 to 28 dorsal vertebrae. The fossil specimen also exhibits key characteristics of juvenile ichthyosaur reptiles, including short forelimbs, incomplete ossification of the humerus and ribs, and unossified wrist bones. After comparing 20 previously reported fossils and conducting morphological and statistical analyses, the researchers found that despite similarities in skull features and vertebral counts, Huphsuchus and Nanchangosaurus differ significantly in several key traits. According to Li Jiangli, head of the joint research team and director of the paleontology center at the Hubei Institute of Geosciences, Yuan’an county hosts a globally rare assemblage of Early Triassic marine reptile fossils, with abundant, exceptionally well-preserved Huphsuchus specimens of significant scientific value. The Yuan’an fauna, together with four other fossil assemblages spanning the Early to Late Triassic, forms a rare, nearly complete evolutionary sequence of Triassic marine reptiles in South China, offering valuable insights into their origins, diversification, evolution and extinction while presenting new scientific challenges, Li said. At present, the joint research team is stepping up the restoration and study of Yuan’an’s prehistoric marine reptile fossils, seeking new insights into their evolution, physiology, behavior and environments in which they lived, Li added.

item.title: Beijing tackles rapid aging as capital expected to become super-aged society by 2035
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 16:08:00
Elderly people relax and chat at Ritan Park in Beijing on October 9, 2026. Photo: IC Beijing is expected to become a super-aged society by 2035, with one-third of its population aged 60 or older. To address this trend, the Chinese capital has stepped up efforts in recent years to strengthen legal protections for elderly care, improve social security, promote the integration of elderly care services with related industries, expand medical-care partnerships and reinforce its multi-tiered pension system, Beijing Daily reported on Saturday. According to data released at a recent industry forum ahead of the Double Ninth Festival, also known as the Chongyang Festival, in Beijing, Beijing had 5.288 million permanent residents aged 60 and above at the end of 2025, accounting for 24.3 percent of its population. The proportion is expected to exceed 33 percent by 2035, meaning one in every three residents will be aged 60 or above, according to Beijing Daily. As a megacity, Beijing is stepping up efforts to address its rapidly aging population. In January, it introduced its first comprehensive, foundational local regulation on elderly care services, making it the first city in China to establish a three-tier elderly care service network covering districts, subdistricts (townships) and communities (villages) through local legislation. Beijing has also raised basic pensions for urban and rural residents year after year and established a system of allowances and subsidies for elderly care services. In 2025, it disbursed about 3.51 billion yuan ($525 million) in such allowances and subsidies, benefiting older people facing financial hardship, those unable to care for themselves and those of advanced age, with a total of 11.958 million beneficiary instances. Meanwhile, Beijing is pursuing an integrated approach to developing elderly care services and related industries. To date, Beijing has 620 registered elderly care institutions, 168 regional care centers and more than 1,500 community care stations, providing a total of 155,000 beds across various types of facilities. In response to the trend toward an increasingly aged population, Beijing prioritizes care for the oldest-old population through preferential services, fee reductions and waivers, regular welfare visits and emergency assistance. Given that the vast majority of older people prefer to age at home, Beijing is continuing to develop a 15-minute elderly care service network. Beijing has nearly 3,000 registered meal service sites serving older residents, covering 90 percent of the city's urban and rural communities. Over the next three years, the city plans to add 30,000 home-based elderly care beds. Official statistics showed that China had 323.38 million people aged 60 and above at the end of 2025, accounting for 23 percent of its population. Rising care needs among older people with disabilities, dementia and those living alone are intensifying demand for care services, while a shortage of professional elderly care workers remains a key challenge, according to the Legal Daily. Global Times

item.title: Olympic champion Tola sets China's fastest marathon time with Beijing victory
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 12:13:00
Runners participate in the Beijing Marathon on October 18, 2026 in Beijing. Photo: Courtesy of Beijing Marathon organizers Ethiopia's reigning Olympic marathon champion Tamirat Tola won the 2026 Beijing Marathon on Sunday in 2:03:10, setting a course record and the fastest time ever recorded at a marathon held in China. The 35-year-old's performance at the Beijing Marathon, which also hosted the National Marathon Championships, beat the previous course record of 2:07:06 by almost four minutes. Tola's winning time surpassed the previous fastest time recorded in a marathon in China, 2:05:35, set by Kenyan runner Philimon Kiptoo Kipchumba at the 2023 Shanghai Marathon. The result also underlined Tola's status as one of the leading marathon runners of his generation. He won the men's marathon at the 2022 World Athletics Championships in 2:05:36, then claimed Olympic gold at the Paris 2024 Games in an Olympic-record time of 2:06:26. With Beijing set to host the 2027 World Athletics Championships, 12 years after the 2015 edition, Tola's record could face a new challenge next year. Rain on Saturday gave way to cool, clear conditions for Sunday's race. The race began at Tian'anmen Square, with 32,000 runners taking part. Tola's record-setting victory set a new benchmark for the Beijing Marathon and brought the fastest marathon time recorded in China into the 2:03 range. The event is one of the country's major mass-participation road races, bringing international elite runners together with domestic competitors. Under the Beijing Marathon's prize policy, the men's and women's champions each receive $50,000. An additional 60,000 yuan ($8,967) is available to a champion who breaks the event's course record. Kenyan runner Sabastian Sawe, who made history in April by becoming the first man to run an official marathon in under 2 hours in London, was also in Beijing during the marathon weekend, according to media reports. He visited Peking University, where he shared his experiences and training insights with the young Chinese runners, offering a message to young runners just starting out: "Stay passionate, be patient and remain disciplined."
